nameStory: The "pignut" name comes from the fact that wild pigs and other animals eagerly devour these sweet, maple-scented nuts that fall in autumn. Unlike some hickory nuts with thick, hard shells, pignut hickories have thinner shells that crack more easily, making them a favorite food for wildlife. The "pig" part isn't because the nuts taste bad to humans – quite the opposite – but because pigs were often turned loose in forests to fatten up on these nutritious treats.
description: Pignut hickory is a tall, stately tree that can grow 60-80 feet high with a straight trunk and an oval crown. It's one of New England's native hickories, sporting the classic compound leaves made up of 5-7 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand. In fall, these leaves turn a beautiful golden yellow that lights up the forest canopy. The tree produces pear-shaped nuts with a distinctive sweet, maple-like smell that makes them easy to identify when you find them on the ground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand (pinnately compound). Each leaflet is oval with fine teeth along the edges and feels smooth to the touch. In fall, they turn a brilliant golden-yellow color.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Pear-shaped nuts that ripen in September and October, enclosed in a thin husk that splits into 4 sections. The nuts have a distinctive sweet, maple-like smell when fresh – take a sniff when you find them on the ground.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Relatively smooth gray bark that doesn't peel or shag like some other hickories. The bark may have shallow furrows but remains fairly tight to the trunk, earning it the nickname 'smoothbark hickory.'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, straight-trunked tree with an oval to rounded crown. Branches tend to be sturdy and don't droop, giving the tree an upright, dignified appearance in the forest.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, brown, and somewhat egg-shaped with overlapping scales. They're much smaller and less noticeable than the large, distinctive buds of shagbark hickory.

habitat: Pignut hickory thrives in the oak-hickory forests throughout New England, preferring well-drained upland sites with rich, deep soils. You'll often find it growing alongside oaks, maples, and other hickories on hillsides and ridges. It's adaptable to various soil conditions but does best in areas that aren't too wet or too dry.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring with a fresh green color. Look for the distinctive compound leaf pattern as leaflets unfold from winter buds.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy of green compound leaves provides excellent identification opportunities. The tree maintains its stately appearance throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant golden-yellow, making the tree easy to spot in mixed forests. Pear-shaped nuts ripen and fall, releasing their sweet maple scent.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's upright growth habit and smooth gray bark. Small brown buds and any remaining nut husks on the ground help with identification.

funFact: Pignut hickory wood is so dense and shock-resistant that it was the preferred material for making axe handles, baseball bats, and even aircraft parts during World War II – the same toughness that helps the tree survive New England's harsh winters makes it perfect for tools that take a beating.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other hickories, especially mockernut hickory. Remember that pignut has smooth bark (not shaggy like shagbark hickory) and smaller buds than mockernut. The sweet maple smell of fresh pignut nuts is also distinctive – give them a sniff test when you find them on the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you – 'pignut' doesn't mean the nuts taste bad to humans. Early settlers actually found them quite palatable, though they're smaller and harder to crack than some other hickory nuts. The name simply refers to their popularity with pigs and other livestock that were turned loose to forage in forests.
compareHints: Pignut hickory has much smoother bark than the dramatically peeling shagbark hickory, and smaller, less noticeable buds than the large, fuzzy-budded mockernut hickory. Its nuts are pear-shaped rather than round like many other hickories, and they have that distinctive sweet maple scent that sets them apart from the more bitter bitternut hickory.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hickories, shagbark is the only one with bark that peels in long, dramatic strips - other hickories have tight, furrowed bark.
Among New England hickories, bitternut is the easiest to identify thanks to its unique yellow buds.

Among New England hickories, mockernut is the only one with consistently fuzzy leaf undersides - shagbark hickory has peeling bark plates, bitternut has bright yellow buds, and pignut has smooth leaves and smaller nuts.

Red hickory differs from shagbark hickory by having smooth bark instead of distinctive shaggy plates, and from pignut hickory by typically having 5 leaflets instead of 7, plus sweeter nuts and reddish inner bark.
Among New England hickories, shellbark stands out for its larger nuts and more dramatic bark peeling compared to shagbark hickory.
